headline: Avoiding fixed-rate bonds entirely in favour of floating-rate notes — duration adds volatility that defeats the defensive purpose of fixed income, while floaters benefit from rising RBA rates
reasoning: Sherwood argues that fixed-rate bonds do not make sense in an environment of consistently rising yields, noting that bond yields keep surprising to the upside. Their bond income fund holds only floating-rate notes and no fixed-rate bonds, by deliberate design. He says the price volatility of fixed-rate bonds as the yield curve shifts defeats the whole purpose of fixed income, which should be defensive, consistent and low volatility. Adding duration removes that low-volatility characteristic. Floating-rate exposure also benefits directly when the RBA moves rates higher.
quote: Fixed rate bonds just don't make sense in an environment where we've got consistent increases in yields and that's not a new theme. There's obviously a lot of talk about it now because bond yields keep surprising everyone as to how far they're going. But for us floating rates has been the focus for a while. In terms of our bond income fund, we only buy floating rate notes in that fund, we don't buy any fixed rate bonds. And that's very, very deliberate. We just don't see the volatility that comes in terms of prices of fixed rate bonds as the yield curve shifts — just defeats the whole purpose of the asset class in our eyes. The asset class of fixed income is supposed to be designed to be defensive, to be consistent and to be low volatility. And by adding duration or adding fixed rate bonds into a portfolio, you essentially remove that low volatility nature of it.

headline: Lenders now hold the power in private credit: capital inflows have slowed, allowing capital holders to demand stronger covenants and wider yields while being selective on deals
reasoning: Sherwood argues that 12 months ago it was a borrower's market with abundant capital chasing deals and borrowers securing very favourable terms. That has now reversed: inflows into private market investments have slowed, so those holding capital are in a 'pre powerful' position. Lenders can now negotiate stronger covenants, wider yields, and can afford to be picky about which deals they fund. He describes this as a clear swing from the environment of a year ago.
quote: I'd say that a year ago it was very much a borrowers market. There was so much capital looking to be put to work. Borrowers, you know, of all sorts of projects as well as corporates were able to negotiate some very, very good terms for how they borrow money. And I think it has shifted. It is now very much I refer to as a lenders market. That is, those that are holding the capital are holding the power. There's still plenty of people looking to borrow, but those with the capital can essentially now negotiate some stronger terms, perhaps on their covenants in their loans or wider yields. And they can afford to be quite picky and choosy as to which deals they fund.

headline: Diversify across public wholesale fixed income, private credit, corporate lending and asset lending rather than concentrating in real estate credit — mid-market corporate exposure offers some of the best risk-reward

He notes that mid-market corporate trades can produce the best risk-reward outcomes and that investors focused solely on property credit are missing those opportunities. As long as you know who you're investing with and you're investing with a strong team that has the right skill set and then having some corporate lending and some asset lending as well. Not just putting all your eggs into perhaps real estate credit, which is obviously been a dominant space in private markets in Australia. But trying to build a portfolio that has a greater cross-section of exposures is a great way to diversify. Some of the best corporate trades out there can produce the best risk reward. So if you're only looking at property related credit, you're missing out on looking at that opportunity. headline: Not all private credit is equal — construction is inherently riskier; diversification across corporate, asset-backed and property sub-sectors is key to managing concentration risk
reasoning: Sherwood argues that recent high-profile collapses (e.g. Baffler in NSW) are not a new phenomenon but rather highlight the dangers of concentration in property-related private credit, which represents roughly 60% of Australian private credit. He distinguishes between riskier construction-focused lending and lower-risk corporate and asset-backed credit. His firm runs roughly one-third allocations across corporate, asset-backed and property, and has largely avoided construction risk. He stresses that manager selection and diversification are the primary mitigants.
quote: I think all these headlines are really highlighting that not all private credit is equal, and it never has been. Construction risk has always been a riskier part of private credit. That is nothing new at all. But what has been really shown, I guess, in some of these headlines is that concentrations of exposures is risky. We don't have any exposure to Baffler. But we've largely avoided construction risk because we have seen some potential headwinds coming in in that sector. But I think also it highlights that selection of your manager is important. And also diversification is important. So, you know, a large percentage of private credit in Australia has been concentrated around property — about 60% of private credit in Australia is property related — whereas there is a lot of other areas of private credit available as well through corporate credit, through asset backed credit.
